title: Stroke in Pregnancy and Preeclampsia: Effect of Low‐Dose Aspirin Treatment on Collateral Flow Velocity and Cerebral Blood Flow Autoregulation During Ischemia in Rats
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.abstract:
Experimental preeclampsia (ePE) has been shown to have worsened outcome from stroke. We investigated the effect of low‐dose aspirin, known to prevent preeclampsia, on stroke hemodynamics and outcome, and the association between the vasoconstrictor and vasodilator cyclooxygenase products thromboxane A 2 and prostacyclin.

Middle cerebral artery occlusion was performed for 3 hours with 1 hour of reperfusion in normal pregnant rats on day 20 of gestation and compared with ePE treated with vehicle or low‐dose aspirin (1.5 mg/kg per day). Multisite laser Doppler was used to measure changes in cerebral blood flow to the core middle cerebral artery and collateral vascular territories. After 30 minutes occlusion, phenylephrine was infused to increase blood pressure and assess cerebral blood flow autoregulation. Infarct and edema were measured using 2,3,5‐triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining. Plasma levels of thromboxane A 2 , prostacyclin, and inflammatory markers in plasma and cyclooxygenase levels in cerebral arteries were measured. ePE had increased infarction compared with normal pregnant rats ( P <0.05) that was reduced by aspirin ( P <0.001). ePE also had intact cerebral blood flow autoregulation and reduced collateral perfusion during induced hypertension that was also prevented by aspirin. Aspirin increased prostacyclin in ePE ( P <0.05) without reducing thromboxane B 2 , metabolite of thromboxane A 2 , or 8‐isoprostane‐prostaglandin‐2α, a marker of lipid peroxidation. There were no differences in cyclooxygenase levels in cerebral arteries between groups.

Low‐dose aspirin in ePE reduced infarction that was associated with increased vasodilator prostacyclin and improved collateral perfusion during induced hypertension. The beneficial effect of aspirin on the brain and cerebral circulation is likely multifactorial and worth further study.
sections.methods:
The data that support the findings of this study are available upon request to the corresponding author.

Rat models of normal pregnancy and ePE were used for all experiments. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Vermont and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals . Rats were randomly assigned to treatment group and experiments were conducted in a randomized fashion. Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments 2.0 guidelines were followed for the reporting of results. We used an established model that involves maintaining pregnant rats on a high cholesterol diet starting on gestational day 7. 29 , 30 , 31 See Data S1 for details.

ePE rats were treated with aspirin (1.5 mg/kg daily) in transgenic dough diet (Bio‐Serv, Flemington, NJ) or vehicle (1 g, dough without aspirin) starting on gestational day 7. This dose of aspirin has been shown in other studies to decrease TXA 2 and cyclooxygenase in models of preeclampsia. 32 , 33 Normal late‐pregnant (LP) rats were used as a control for ePE and treated with vehicle. Table S1 lists body weights, blood glucoses, and water consumption for all groups of animals.

Pup and placenta weights were measured postmortem on gestational day 20. Uterine horns were first examined for total number of pups and any reabsorbed fetuses. To assess any growth restrictions, fetuses and their placentas were individually weighed and recorded.

Temporary filament occlusion of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) was used, as described previously. 20 , 23 Animals experienced 3 hours of ischemia followed by 1 hour of reperfusion. See Data S1 for details. Table S2 lists blood gases and pH for all animals before and during transient MCA occlusion. To measure changes of CBF velocity in the MCA core ischemic and collateral vascular territories, multisite laser Doppler was used (Figure 1A ), as previously published. 20 , 23 This method measures continuous changes in CBF velocity, not absolute values, simultaneous with arterial blood pressure. See Data S1 for details. Arterial blood pressure was continuously measured via femoral artery catheter connected to an inline pressure transducer.

A , Coronal brain section from a rat showing laser Doppler probe placement. Probe 1 measured changes in core MCA CBF velocity and Probe 2 measured changes in collateral CBF velocity between the ACA and MCA vascular territories. B , Timeline of experimental interventions. Changes in CBF velocity and arterial blood pressure were measured at baseline before filament insertion and then for 30 minutes after filament removal for reperfusion. ACA indicates anterior cerebral artery; CBF, cerebral blood flow; MCA, middle cerebral artery; and Phen, phenylephrine.

After 30 minutes of filament occlusion of the MCA, phenylephrine (5 mg/mL in saline) was infused intravenously to increase baseline blood pressure by ~30% for 10 minutes (Figure 1B ). MCA and collateral CBF velocity were continuously monitored before, during and after pressor therapy with multisite laser Doppler simultaneously with blood pressure via femoral artery catheter. Data were sampled every minute and the relationship between changes in MCA and collateral flow with blood pressure in response to pressor therapy was used to measure the effectiveness of CBF autoregulation, as previously done. 34

At the completion of reperfusion, animals were euthanized by rapid decapitation under isoflurane anesthesia (2% in oxygen). The brains were carefully removed and coronally sectioned into 2 mm sections. Infarct volume was determined by 2,3,5‐triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining, identified as white area of each section and measured with ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD), as previously described. 20 , 23 Measurements were made by investigators who were blinded to experimental groups.

At the completion of the experiment and before sectioning for triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining, MCAs were dissected from the contralateral side to occlusion, snap frozen, and stored at −80 °C until use. Western blot analysis was used to measure cyclooxygenase‐1 and cyclooxygenase‐2 protein levels. See Data S1 for details.

Blood samples were obtained for each rat and collected plasma tubes containing sodium citrate. Plasma was stored at −80 °C until use. Plasma levels of 8‐isoprostane‐prostaglandin‐2α (8‐iso‐PGF2α), prostacyclin, thromboxane B 2 (TXB 2 ), and TNF‐α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) levels were measured by commercially available ELISA using manufacturer's instructions. See Data S1 for details.

One LP animal was removed from infarct and edema measurements as a statistical outlier.

Results are presented as mean±SEM. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 10.1.2 software (GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla, CA). Normal distribution of data was determined by Kolmogorov–Smirnov or D'Agostino & Pearson normality tests. Differences between groups were determined by either 2‐way repeated measures ANOVA or 2‐way ANOVA without repeated measures or mixed model ANOVA and a post hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons test for data not normally distributed. Pearson r correlation was used to determine the correlation between changes in CBF velocity and arterial blood pressure as a measure of CBF autoregulation effectiveness. 34 Arterial blood pressures and changes in CBF velocity were sampled every minute and replicates averaged before correlation analysis. 34 Differences were considered significant at P <0.05. The number of animals used in each experiment was determined by statistical power calculation based on our previous studies using similar methodology. 20
sections.results:
Filament occlusion of the MCA caused a rapid drop in velocity of both MCA and collateral CBF in all groups that was similar. Table 1 shows the % change in CBF velocity in both vascular territories from baseline with filament insertion and removal. Figure S1 shows the average % change in CBF velocity for both MCA and collateral vascular territories over the entire ischemic and reperfusion periods. The % decrease in CBF velocity was similar between groups, although the decrease was less in the collateral versus MCA territory. Removal of the filament after 180 minutes of ischemia caused relatively complete yet variable reperfusion in all animals that was similar between groups.

Change in MCA and Collateral CBF From Baseline

CBF indicates cerebral blood flow; ePE, experimental preeclampsia; and MCA, middle cerebral artery.

After 30 minutes of occlusion, phenylephrine was infused to temporarily raise blood pressure. Figure 2A shows blood pressure before and during ischemia in all groups of animals. Phenylephrine increased blood pressure similarly in all groups. Aspirin treatment of ePE reduced arterial blood pressure during ischemia that was significantly lower compared with LP ( P <0.01). Figure 2B and 2C show the change in MCA and collateral flow velocity in response to occlusion and pressor therapy, that is, CBF velocity was normalized to just after filament occlusion so that the change in CBF velocity shown was during ischemia. Both LP and ePE, but not ePE+aspirin, had an initial increase in MCA flow velocity in response to occlusion; however, the increase in CBF velocity with filament occlusion was transient in ePE animals, but remained elevated in LP ( P <0.01). When phenylephrine was given to increase arterial blood pressure, MCA flow velocity increased substantially more in LP than ePE and ePE+aspirin groups. In addition, MCA flow velocity remained elevated in LP animals over the course of ischemia. Although ePE and ePE+aspirin also increased MCA flow velocity in response to phenylephrine, the increase was less than LP and transient, returning to the level before phenylephrine infusion.

A , Arterial blood pressure measured by arterial catheter during the MCA occlusion surgery in all groups. Phenylephrine was infused intravenously 30 minutes into occlusion that increased blood pressure in all groups. Over the remaining ischemic duration, aspirin‐treated ePE animals had lower blood pressure than LP (* P <0.05, ** P <0.01 ePE+aspirin vs LP by mixed‐effects analysis, row factor F [4.156, 71.17]=16.64). Percentage of change in ( B ) MCA CBF velocity and ( C ) collateral CBF velocity normalized from just after filament insertion to measure changes in CBF during occlusion. MCA CBF velocity increased after filament insertion significantly in LP (* P =0.035, ** P =0.0076 ePE+aspirin vs LP by repeated measures ANOVA, row factor F [1.387, 26.36]=3.623, df=18). Similarly, CBF velocity increased in the collateral circulation in LP (* P <0.05, ** P <0.01 ePE+aspirin vs LP by repeated measures ANOVA, row factor F [1.663, 31.60]=6.786, df=18) but not aspirin treated. The increase in CBF velocity with occlusion was sustained in LP and transient in ePE. CBF indicates cerebral blood flow; ePE, experimental preeclampsia; ePE+asp, ePE+aspirin; LP, late‐pregnant; MCA, middle cerebral artery; and Phen, phenylephrine.

Figure 2C shows the change in collateral flow velocity in response to occlusion and pressor therapy while the filament was in place. Collateral flow velocity increased in both LP and ePE animals, but not ePE+aspirin, during the first 20 minutes of occlusion. Infusion of phenylephrine caused an increase in collateral CBF velocity during occlusion in LP and ePE but not in ePE+aspirin animals, although this was not statistically significant.

Figure 3A and 3B show the percentage of infarction and edema formation, respectively, in all groups of animals. ePE animals had significantly greater infarction and edema than LP animals ( P <0.05 for infarction and P <0.01 for edema). Aspirin treatment of ePE animals prevented the increase in infarction and edema as they were similar to LP. The calculated effect size (Cohen's d ) for each comparison was ≈1.034 for LP versus ePE; ≈0.508 for LP versus ePE+aspirin; and ≈0.526 for ePE versus ePE+aspirin. Figure 3C shows representative coronal brain sections stained with triphenyltetrazolium chloride demonstrating infarction in all groups of animals.

A , Percentage of infarction and ( B ) percentage of edema in all groups by TTC. ePE animals had increased infarction (* P <0.05 vs LP by 2‐way ANOVA, column factor F [2, 12]=4.240, df=2) and edema (* P <0.01 vs LP by 2‐way repeated measured ANOVA, column factor F [2, 12]=7.325, df=2). Aspirin treatment of ePE animals prevented the increase in infarct and edema that was not different than LP. C , Representative TTC images showing coronally sliced brains from all groups of animals. The white regions are areas of infarction surrounded by healthy red tissue. ePE indicates experimental preeclampsia; ePE+asp, ePE+aspirin; LP, late‐pregnant; and TTC, triphenyltetrazolium chloride.

The effectiveness of pressor therapy depends on the collateral circulation having impaired CBF autoregulation, that is, pressure passive, to hemodynamically enhance CBF. We therefore assessed CBF autoregulation during ischemia in response to the increase in blood pressure induced by phenylephrine. Figure 4 shows the average percent change in CBF velocity in the MCA and collateral territories in response to increasing blood pressure with phenylephrine while the filament was occluding the MCA in all groups of animals. In both LP (Figure 4A ) and ePE+aspirin (Figure 4C ) treated animals, MCA and collateral perfusion increased with increased blood pressure, suggesting vasodilation that enhanced CBF velocity. This response was largely absent in ePE animals in which MCA perfusion transiently increased with increased blood pressure (Figure 4 ), and collateral perfusion did not change at all.

The percentage of change in CBF velocity in both vascular territories together with blood pressure is shown for ( A ) LP+veh, ( B ) ePE+veh, and ( C ) ePE+asp groups. CBF, cerebral blood flow; ePE, experimental preeclampsia; ePE+asp, ePE+aspirin; and Phen ON, phenylephrine on.

To determine the degree of correlation between the change in CBF velocity and arterial blood pressure, a Pearson's correlation was done. Table 2 shows Pearson's r values and P values between the change in MCA perfusion, collateral perfusion, and arterial blood pressure. In all groups, there was a robust and significant correlation between the change MCA CBF velocity with arterial blood pressure, suggesting this vascular territories had impaired CBF autoregulation, that is, CBF was mostly pressure passive. In the collateral circulation that perfuses the penumbra, LP animals had high correlation with blood pressure. In contrast, there was no correlation between collateral flow velocity and arterial blood pressure in ePE animals ( r =0.07) demonstrating highly intact CBF autoregulation in the collateral territory. In ePE animals treated with aspirin, CBF autoregulation in the collateral circulation was almost entirely absent (impaired). Thus, ePE animals appeared to have vasoconstricted collateral vessels that limited perfusion in response to phenylephrine whereas aspirin treatment promoted vasodilation that increased collateral perfusion.

Pearson r Value Correlation Between Blood Pressure and Change in Blood Pressure

ePE indicates experimental preeclampsia; and MCA, middle cerebral artery.

To determine the effect of ePE and aspirin treatment on cyclooxygenase‐1 and cyclooxygenase‐2 in cerebral arteries, a Western blot was done using pooled MCAs from the contralateral side to occlusion. Figure S2A shows a representative Western blot for cyclooxygenase‐1 and cyclooxygenase‐2. Figures S2B and S2C show the relative expression of cyclooxygenase‐1 and cyclooxygenase‐2 protein levels in MCAs. There was no difference in either cyclooxygenase‐1 or cyclooxygenase‐2 protein in MCAs between any of the groups.

Figure 5 shows plasma levels of the cyclooxygenase products TXB 2 , prostacyclin, and inflammatory markers. Plasma levels of prostacyclin, were nonsignificantly decreased in ePE compared with normal pregnant animals (Figure 5A ). Aspirin treatment increased prostacyclin ( P <0.05) that was significantly greater in ePE+aspirin versus ePE. TXB 2 , a stable metabolite of TXA 2 , was increased in both ePE groups compared with LP ( P <0.05 versus ePE and P <0.001 versus ePE+aspirin) that was not ameliorated with aspirin treatment (Figure 5B ). In addition, 8‐iso‐PGF2α was also increased in both ePE groups irrespective of aspirin treatment (Figure 5C ; P <0.05 versus ePE and P <0.01 versus ePE+aspirin). However, plasma levels of the inflammatory marker TNFα were not different between groups (Figure 5D ).

Plasma levels of ( A ) PGI 2 , ( B ) TXB 2 , a stable metabolite of TXA 2 , ( C ) 8‐iso‐PGF2α, a marker of lipid peroxidation, and ( D ) TNFα, a marker of inflammation. All samples were taken after stroke. PGI2 was elevated ePE+aspirin treated animals (* P <0.05 vs ePE by one‐way ANOVA). TXB 2 and 8‐iso‐PGF2α were elevated in ePE animals that was not prevented by aspirin (* P <0.05, ** P <0.01 and *** P <0.001 vs LP by 1‐way ANOVA). Plasma TNFα levels were not different between the groups. 8‐iso‐PGF2α indicates 8‐isoprostane‐prostaglandin‐2α; ePE, experimental preeclampsia; ePE+asp, ePE+aspirin; LP, late‐pregnant; PGI 2 TNFα, tumor necrosis factor alpha; TXA 2 , thromboxane A2; and TXB 2 , thromboxane B2.

There were no significant differences in litter size between LP, ePE and ePE+aspirin groups (13±0.4, 13±0.5, 13±0.8, respectively). There was no difference in pup weights or placenta weights between groups (Figure 6A and 6B ).

A , Pup weights were not different between groups. B , Placental weights were nonsignificantly increased in ePE and ePE+aspirin compared with LP. ePE indicates experimental preeclampsia; ePE+asp, ePE+aspirin; and LP, late‐pregnant.
sections.discussion:
In the current study, we treated ePE animals with low‐dose aspirin to investigate the role of inflammation, oxidative stress, and the balance between prostacyclin and TXA 2 in stroke outcome and mediating cerebral hemodynamics during stroke. We found that ePE animals had increased infarction compared with normal LP animals that was prevented by aspirin treatment. The reduced early infarction in both LP and aspirin‐treated ePE animals was associated with a greater cerebral vasodilatory state that increased perfusion in response to increased blood pressure with phenylephrine. This impaired autoregulation potentially enhanced perfusion to the penumbra driven by increased blood pressure with phenylephrine. The more vasodilatory “passive” state of the cerebral circulation in ePE+aspirin animals could have been due to increased prostacyclin. In contrast, ePE animals had poor collateral flow in response to phenylephrine that may have been due to increased TXA 2 that was not counteracted by prostacyclin. Interestingly, the enhanced collateral perfusion in ePE animals treated with aspirin was associated with increased prostacyclin levels without a change in TXB 2 (TXA 2 ) or 8‐iso‐PGF2α, a marker of lipid peroxidation, that were both elevated in ePE animals. Thus, the beneficial effect of low‐dose aspirin treatment of ePE on stroke outcome appeared more related to an enhanced vasodilatory state that promoted a pressure‐passive CBFAR response than reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

We used pressor therapy as both a means to increase collateral CBF velocity as well as assess CBFAR in the different vascular territories during occlusion. We found impaired CBFAR in both MCA and collateral vascular territories in LP animals as shown by a strong correlation between arterial blood pressure and change in CBF velocity, that is, CBF was largely pressure passive in those regions. In ePE animals, MCA CBF velocity was also mostly pressure passive showing impaired CBFAR, but largely intact in the collateral circulation. In fact, there was no correlation between change in CBF velocity and arterial blood pressure ( r =0.07) in the collateral circulation of ePE rats. The lack of a vasodilatory response to elevated blood pressure in the collateral circulation of ePE animals could contribute to worse outcome through myogenic vasoconstriction that limited CBF to the penumbra. We previously showed that pial collaterals responded to increased pressure with robust myogenic vasoconstriction in a model of chronic hypertension, an effect that was not seen in normotensive animals. 21 It is possible that PE had a similar effect on collaterals, decreasing collateral perfusion during stroke and increasing infarction. Aspirin treatment of ePE animals prevented this vasoconstriction and caused both MCA and collateral flow to be almost completely pressure passive, with high correlation between change in CBF velocity and arterial pressure ( r =0.98 and 0.91, respectively). This suggests aspirin treatment had a vasodilatory effect on the cerebral circulation that prevented myogenic vasoconstriction and allowed for hemodynamically increased CBF during pressor therapy. This lack of vasoconstriction to increased pressure was possibly due to increased prostacyclin and not inhibition of TXA 2 that remained elevated. Low‐dose aspirin has been shown to promote vasodilation and increase perfusion in the uteroplacental circulation during pregnancy that was associated with reduced fetal growth restriction and placental infarction. 35 , 36 The results of the current study suggest the beneficial effect of aspirin treatment extends to the brain and cerebral circulation to improve stroke outcome in ePE animals.

In the present study, we did not find any hemorrhagic transformation despite the disease state of ePE or aspirin use even with 3 hours of ischemia with reperfusion. In a previous study, we found that nonpregnant animals had a high incidence of hemorrhage with this duration of ischemia. 20 In that study, hemorrhagic transformation was absent in both normal pregnant and ePE animals, suggesting pregnancy alone was protective of hemorrhage as ePE animals were pregnant as well. In the present study, that protection persisted even in the presence of aspirin treatment suggesting this was not related to changes in hemostasis. Pregnancy is a state of high levels of reproductive hormones that may have a protective effect on the brain. For example, estrogen and progesterone are produced in high levels during pregnancy and known to be neuroprotective in stroke, including preventing hemorrhagic transformation. 37 , 38 The protective nature of pregnancy during stroke was recently found in a clinical study. Compared with nonpregnant age‐matched women with stroke, the risk of death in pregnant patients was lower up to 1 year post stroke, and readmission for vascular events was substantially less. 5 This protection was lost after a year postpartum, suggesting high levels of sex steroids produced during pregnancy may have contributed. However, there may be multiple mechanisms for pregnancy‐related protection from stroke injury during the early phase after stroke, an understanding of which may provide unique therapeutic targets for other stroke populations.

All groups of animals had a surprising increase in core MCA flow in response to increased blood pressure with phenylephrine infusion that was equal to or greater than the change in collateral flow. Because the change was measured while the filament was in place, the increase in MCA flow was attributed to collateral flow. It is possible that collaterals from the posterior cerebral artery territory in addition to anterior cerebral artery‐MCA collaterals contributed to increasing MCA flow. A previous study by Shin et al that measured changes in both anterior cerebral artery ACA‐MCA and posterior cerebral artery‐MCA collateral flow during pressor therapy found that both increased. 39 In addition, LP animals had a sustained increase in CBF velocity after pressor therapy, most notably in the MCA core infarct territory, that likely contributed to reduced infarct in those animals.

Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase pathway generated as part of arachidonic acid metabolism and decreases generation of TXA 2 . 24 , 25 In the current study, we did not find a decrease in cyclooxygenase‐1 or cyclooxygenase‐2 in cerebral arteries. This result suggests that aspirin treatment affected the activity of the cyclooxygenase enzymes without affecting the level of expression. Aspirin has also been shown to have direct antioxidant effects on the vasculature and reduce lipid peroxidation. 40 , 41 In the present study, aspirin did not appear to prevent oxidative stress as levels of 8‐iso‐PGF2α, a marker of lipid peroxidation, were increased in ePE animals regardless of aspirin treatment. A limitation of this study is that we did not measure cyclooxygenase activity or other markers of vascular inflammation that could have contributed to worsened outcome in ePE.

PE is a complex disease that has long‐lasting effects extending beyond pregnancy through increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline later in life. The pleotropic actions of aspirin likely underlie its beneficial effect in preventing PE, including increased perfusion to the uteroplacental vascular bed. 13 , 14 , 35 , 36 Here we showed an additional beneficial effect of aspirin treatment in PE, that of reducing acute ischemic brain injury. The mechanism by which aspirin improved stroke outcome in ePE is more related to vasodilation and promoting a pressure‐passive state that improved CBF velocity during pressor therapy as opposed to preventing platelet activation or reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.
sections.conclusion: PE is a complex disease that has long‐lasting effects extending beyond pregnancy through increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline later in life. The pleotropic actions of aspirin likely underlie its beneficial effect in preventing PE, including increased perfusion to the uteroplacental vascular bed. 13 , 14 , 35 , 36 Here we showed an additional beneficial effect of aspirin treatment in PE, that of reducing acute ischemic brain injury. The mechanism by which aspirin improved stroke outcome in ePE is more related to vasodilation and promoting a pressure‐passive state that improved CBF velocity during pressor therapy as opposed to preventing platelet activation or reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.
